title: Environmental Science

jokes.text: What? First, we give a month to black history, now seven days on the Irish.
jokes.setup: The dean announces 'Green Week' at the school.
jokes.punchline: Pierce mishears or misinterprets 'Green Week' as being about Irish people, conflating it with identity-history months — revealing his obliviousness in a single breath.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical Pierce joke: one sentence reveals his racism-adjacent ignorance, his competitive grievance-tracking of minority recognition months, and his complete failure to understand the concept being announced. The 'month to black history / seven days on the Irish' parallel structure does the heavy lifting and the logic is internally consistent in Pierce's worldview.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I'm proud to announce that Greendale Community College is officially changing its name to Envirodale Community College. It's more earth-smart.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: Dean, we were already called Greendale.

jokes.text: We're changing our name to Envirodale. / But we were already called Greendale.
jokes.setup: The dean proudly announces the school's new 'green' rebranding to 'Envirodale.'
jokes.punchline: Someone points out the school was already called 'Greendale' — the rebranding is redundant and the dean has apparently missed the obvious.
jokes.explanation: Clean, tight joke about institutional stupidity. The setup is the dean's earnest enthusiasm and the punchline is devastatingly simple. Works because it characterizes the dean's obliviousness without needing to announce it. The beat of silence after the callout (inferred from the [00:33] timestamp) adds to the comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Green Day is coming to perform at Greendale!

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: Oh.

jokes.text: There's also going to be a free rock 'n' roll concert by a certain band called Green Day.
jokes.setup: Dean tries to redeem the awkward Green Week announcement by teasing a surprise.
jokes.punchline: He calls them 'a certain band called Green Day' as if this is an exotic, mysterious announcement — but then the band turns out to be a fake knock-off called 'Greene Daeye.'
jokes.explanation: Plant joke that pays off later when the band is revealed to be a fake. On first watch, the reveal that it's the real Green Day gets a mild reaction, but the later payoff (Greene Daeye) recontextualizes this. Gets a rewatch bonus because the setup is better than it initially appears.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: We need to reprint 5,000 more flyers. We're going green!

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I'm saving the planet.

jokes.text: That make you happy? / No, not really.
jokes.setup: Dean expects the Green Day announcement to generate excitement.
jokes.punchline: The flat 'No, not really' — the audience's total indifference to what should be a great perk.
jokes.explanation: Functional deflation joke. Works in the rhythm of the scene but doesn't have much identity of its own.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: Wait, why doesn't Annie have to write the essay?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Because Annie's a kiss-up. But you know what? Fine. Everyone writes an essay. The essay title is: 'Why I Will Not Commit Acts of Violence Against Professor Chang.'

jokes.text: We need to re-do these. / We printed 5000. / Well, print 5000 more. I'm trying to save a planet here.
jokes.setup: Flyers have already been printed; the dean wants them redone.
jokes.punchline: The dean instructs them to print 5000 MORE flyers — massively wasteful — while claiming to be saving the planet.
jokes.explanation: Sharp irony joke with a tight structure. The hypocrisy is the punchline and it's delivered with straight-faced conviction. The phrase 'I'm trying to save a planet here' as justification for printing 10,000 flyers is excellent deadpan writing. Earns a high score because it also satirizes performative environmentalism broadly.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: I don't really know much Spanish.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Perfect. Write a five-page essay on why you don't know Spanish.

jokes.text: Annie is caught doing something (implied cheating or rule-breaking) and Chang assigns the whole class 'Annie's Mistake' as a one-page essay.
jokes.setup: Annie is caught doing something; Chang calls her out.
jokes.punchline: Instead of just punishing Annie, Chang assigns a humiliating essay titled 'Annie's Mistake' to the whole class — maximum public shaming.
jokes.explanation: Chang's punishment style is perfectly absurdist-authoritarian. Naming the essay after the student's mistake is specific, petty, and deeply revealing of Chang's character — it's not just extra homework, it's public humiliation as pedagogy.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Chang, I think if we all just take a step back and approach this calmly and rationally...

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Ass-kissing! That's what that is! You know what? I'm quadrupling the assignment.

jokes.text: Why doesn't Annie have to write it? / Okay, two pages, entitled: 'The Consequences of Questioning Authority.'
jokes.setup: Student reasonably points out that Annie is exempt from her own punitive essay.
jokes.punchline: Chang escalates the punishment — now two pages — with a title that is itself the punishment. The title of the essay IS the lesson he's forcing on the student.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation structure. Chang's response is both petty and self-parodying — the title 'The Consequences of Questioning Authority' IS the punishment, delivered as if he's doing them a pedagogical favor. Tight and character-specific: only Chang would do this.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Chang, you can't just keep doing increasingly unhinged things and expect—

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I'm going to win a Grammy!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: A Grammy? Chang, you don't even play music.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Not a Grammy. A Granny. I'm going to be so crazy, they'll just give me an award for being someone's insane grandmother.

jokes.text: This is Spanish. I know how to say 'hello,' 'tomorrow' and tables are female. That's the only Spanish you taught us. / Oh! Six pages on ignorance.
jokes.setup: A student points out that Chang hasn't actually taught them enough Spanish to write the essay.
jokes.punchline: Chang's response — six pages on 'ignorance' — is both another escalation and a perfect ironic reversal (the student's legitimate complaint is reframed as the student's fault).
jokes.explanation: One of the best Chang jokes in the episode. The student's complaint is completely valid — 'tables are female' is a perfect, specific detail that makes the inadequacy of Chang's teaching tangible. Chang's response (six pages on ignorance) doesn't refute the complaint at all — it weaponizes it. The escalating essay-title punishment structure is now fully established as a running gag. High originality because the punchline operates on two levels: it's a continuation of the escalation pattern AND an ironic deflection.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You're afraid of rats.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'm not afraid of rats. I just don't associate with them. They're poor.

jokes.text: Guys, put your hands down. Señor Chang, please continue. We respect your authority. / Thank you, Britta. Twenty pages on ass kissing.
jokes.setup: Jeff tries to defuse Chang by telling everyone to back off and complimenting Chang's authority — essentially doing what Chang wants.
jokes.punchline: Chang punishes Britta anyway — now for ass kissing — completing the logical trap: challenge authority, get punished. Respect it, also get punished.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Kafka trap — the escalating essay game reveals there is no winning move. 'Twenty pages on ass kissing' is a great line because it's crass and academic simultaneously, and it shows Chang is not applying a principle — he's just punishing everyone. The 'twenty pages' escalation from six is also structurally satisfying.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You can't just adopt a popular animal. Everyone wants a dog or a cat. You gotta go with something unpopular. Like a koala or a llama.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: And you definitely can't adopt a lake. Lakes are the most unpopular animals of all.

jokes.text: If Señor Chang gets any crazier, he's gonna win the Grammy award.
jokes.setup: The group is reeling from Chang's absurd homework escalation.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's non-sequitur hyperbole — 'win the Grammy' — as a descriptor for insanity is oddly specific and doesn't quite make sense, which is partly the joke.
jokes.explanation: Mildly amusing in the moment. The joke gets a rewatch bonus because it's repeated later in the episode and upgraded ('put on The View'), which makes it a subtle running gag about Jeff's failed attempts at witty analogies. On its own, it's not particularly sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I'll do it.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: What? I always do this. I'm the Annie. In every group, there's an Annie, and the Annie does the weird stuff nobody else wants to do.

jokes.text: I can't write a 20-page paper. I got a presentation in Marketing. And public speaking gives me the nervous sweats. / I can help you with that. I accept. / That's how messed up things are.
jokes.setup: Shirley mentions public speaking gives her the nervous sweats; Pierce immediately volunteers to help.
jokes.punchline: Shirley immediately accepts Pierce's offer — and then Abed's dry aside 'That's how messed up things are' frames the absurdity: the situation is so bad that Pierce helping Shirley seems reasonable.
jokes.explanation: Three-beat joke with Abed's cold commentary as the punchline. 'That's how messed up things are' is a great Abed line — meta, analytical, and funny because it's delivered as pure observation. The joke works because the audience understands Pierce is not a good coach, so Shirley accepting his offer is a commentary on how desperate the situation is.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Jeff's silver tongue? I'd like to get my hands on that silver tongue. Work it like a lollipop.

jokes.text: Troy's afraid of... / I'm not afraid, Abed. I choose not to be around rats because they are unpopular. Same goes for centipedes and lakes.
jokes.setup: Abed starts to reveal Troy's fear of rats.
jokes.punchline: Troy reframes his fear as a social preference — 'rats are unpopular' — and then extends the absurd logic to centipedes AND lakes, which makes no sense.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Troy's coping mechanism — reframing fear as social curation — is specific, absurd, and characterologically perfect for a former jock trying to maintain his image. 'Same goes for centipedes and lakes' is the killer escalation: including 'lakes' in the list of things he avoids because they're 'unpopular' is completely unhinged and deeply funny. It also sets up the entire Troy/rat subplot. High originality, high quotability, strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Look, if I can't convince you guys not to make me do this, how am I supposed to convince Chang?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait... you just did.

jokes.text: Someone has to go to Chang and talk to him. / I vote we all look at Jeff at the same time.
jokes.setup: The group agrees someone needs to confront Chang.
jokes.punchline: Instead of a discussion or vote, the solution is simply for everyone to silently look at Jeff simultaneously — as if he's the obvious choice and this is a formal democratic process.
jokes.explanation: Economical and confident joke. The phrasing 'I vote we all look at Jeff at the same time' is funny because it's couched in procedural language for something that's pure social pressure. It also acknowledges the group's dynamic honestly.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Chang's not crazy, he's just... Chang.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: He's won a Grammy and lost his mind. That's the Chang span.

jokes.text: In a way, all of you are right. / What was I tuning out?
jokes.setup: Jeff apparently tuned out the entire discussion about their problem.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's first contribution is a fake-diplomatic 'In a way, all of you are right,' which is revealed as meaningless when he immediately asks what he missed.
jokes.explanation: Good Jeff characterization: he deploys his smooth social skills reflexively even when he has zero information. 'In a way, all of you are right' is a perfect empty-calorie diplomat line. The immediate follow-up reveals he was bluffing. Well-structured two-beat joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So you guys are doing my homework, right?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: No, Jeff. You're a handsome hobo and we're the end of the line.

jokes.text: What makes you think I could convince Chang if I can't even convince you not to make me do it?
jokes.setup: The group pressures Jeff to go talk to Chang using his silver tongue.
jokes.punchline: Jeff points out the logical flaw: he's failing to persuade them right now, which undermines the premise.
jokes.explanation: Smart self-aware joke. The logic is airtight and the delivery is fast. It's the kind of joke that reveals Jeff's intelligence while also showing he's looking for any exit ramp. Good structure.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, I'll talk to Chang.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Great! We can go to my office.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Your office? The last guy who went to your office came out... different. Actually, he didn't come out.

jokes.text: Jeff does raise a good point. / Wait. You are convincing. / You could do it.
jokes.setup: Jeff makes a logical argument for why he shouldn't have to do it.
jokes.punchline: The group uses his persuasiveness as evidence he SHOULD do it — the meta-joke that Jeff's convincing argument against going is proof he can go.
jokes.explanation: Nice logical trap. The group is basically saying 'you've already proved it, now go do it.' It's a callback to the previous joke's setup, completing the irony — Jeff's argument becomes its own refutation.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Oh my... is that leather? And are those... chains? My goodness, this is highly inappropriate and yet I find myself completely unable to look away.

jokes.text: You want me to risk the C that I'm pulling in that psycho's class by putting myself on his radar? I mean, that guy goes any more nuts, he's gonna win a Grammy.
jokes.setup: Jeff continues to resist going to Chang.
jokes.punchline: Jeff repeats the Grammy line — now it's established as his go-to hyperbole, suggesting he's been workshopping this joke.
jokes.explanation: The repetition of the Grammy line retroactively makes it funnier — it's Jeff's bit, and he keeps using it. Not strong on its own but gains value as part of the running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Ladies and gentlemen, please welcome to Greendale's Green Week celebration... Green Day!

dialogue.speaker: Fake Green Day member
dialogue.line: Actually, we're 'Green... Day.' Get it? Because it's green... and it's day?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's the worst thing I've ever heard.

jokes.text: Because I have you guys. / Well, guess what, handsome hobo? Your gravy train's leaving the station.
jokes.setup: Jeff admits he pulls a C because the group does his work.
jokes.punchline: Britta calls him a 'handsome hobo' and tells him the gravy train is leaving — a vivid, slightly absurd insult that nails Jeff's freeloading charm.
jokes.explanation: 'Handsome hobo' is a great insult — it acknowledges Jeff's attractiveness while calling him a parasite. The 'gravy train' metaphor extends it pleasingly. High quotability because it's the kind of specific, slightly dated-sounding insult that Community characters use. It also neatly characterizes both Jeff (charming freeloader) and Britta (self-righteous but clever).

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Can I ask you a personal question?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Oh, Freud, sure. Psychoanalyze away.

jokes.text: Fine, I'll do it. But when you find my body, don't believe the suicide note.
jokes.setup: Jeff reluctantly agrees to confront Chang.
jokes.punchline: He frames his capitulation as a death sentence and pre-emptively asks that his suicide note be disbelieved — implying Chang will force him to write a note framing the death as self-inflicted.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The dark humor is perfectly calibrated — it's not gratuitous, it characterizes both Jeff's flair for drama and his genuine fear of Chang. 'Don't believe the suicide note' implies Chang will stage it, which is a whole conspiracy theory compressed into six words. Extremely quotable, economical, and funny because of what it doesn't explain. The craft here is in the specificity of 'don't believe the note' vs a generic 'I might die' joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Chang taught them that 'wife' means 'liar' - revealing his bitter feelings

jokes.text: This better not awaken anything in me.
jokes.setup: Chang is about to meet with Jeff one-on-one; he's just agreed to something.
jokes.punchline: Chang's private aside — 'This better not awaken anything in me' — implies he's worried about an attraction to Jeff or some other disturbing internal response.
jokes.explanation: Economically brilliant. Nine words of pure Chang weirdness. The joke works because it's unprompted and self-directed — Chang is policing his own responses, which implies those responses are genuinely a problem. It could be read as attraction, as homicidal impulse, or as admiration — the ambiguity is the richness. Very quotable, very specific to Chang's character.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I satisfy my wife greatly. She's very happy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Well, you have to compensate somehow.

jokes.text: Green Day is here. Wow. / We're Greene Daeye.
jokes.setup: The dean promised Green Day. Jeff sees them and seems impressed.
jokes.punchline: The band reveals they're 'Greene Daeye' — a knock-off — and the dean has apparently been deceived or just doesn't care.
jokes.explanation: Payoff of the planted Green Day joke. The name 'Greene Daeye' is funny as a fake-band name — it's recognizable enough to register as a parody but different enough to be its own thing. The dean's credulous 'Thank you. Oh.' suggests he either already knew or is too defeated to react.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I may be going through a divorce, but I am still very much a man. A man who is skilled in the art of... intimate relations. I have demonstrated considerable proficiency in the horizontal tango, if you will.

jokes.text: What do you want, Winger? You complaining about the homework on behalf of the class?
jokes.setup: Jeff visits Chang's office.
jokes.punchline: Chang immediately reads Jeff's intent with total accuracy, puncturing any chance of manipulation — Chang knows exactly what this is.
jokes.explanation: Functional scene-entry joke. Chang's sharpness here is good characterization — he's not as crazy as he seems — but it's not a standout joke.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Pickled bull testicle?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Are you offering me food or asking me to provide testicles?

jokes.text: Okay, Freud. Sure, you try to penetrate my psychological armor and you...
jokes.setup: Jeff asks Chang a 'personal question.'
jokes.punchline: Chang immediately calls the technique, naming it ('Freud,' 'psychological armor') and beginning to explain it — only to be stopped mid-sentence by Jeff actually landing on the truth.
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the wife-reveal joke. Chang's self-awareness about manipulation attempts is itself funny, and the sentence being cut off mid-analysis because Jeff just goes straight for the truth is a good structural choice.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'm not afraid of rats. I can handle this.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Okay.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: AHHHHHHH! GET IT AWAY FROM ME! OH MY GOD!

jokes.text: Did your wife leave you? / Holy... / How'd you know?
jokes.setup: Chang was mid-explanation about his psychological defenses.
jokes.punchline: Jeff cuts straight through with 'Did your wife leave you?' — which lands perfectly — and Chang's reaction ('Holy...') and genuine surprise are the comedy.
jokes.explanation: Great puncture moment. Jeff's directness is both a character note (he uses a legal/jury-selection mindset to cut through social pretense) and structurally satisfying as a reversal of the expectation Chang was setting up. Chang's stunned reaction sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Don't come near me! I will fight every single one of you!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'm not coming down there!

jokes.text: Same shirt twice in one week. Teaching us the word esposa means 'liar.' A picture of you with a woman with a Post-it note dialogue balloon above her head that says, 'Enjoy it while it lasts.'
jokes.setup: Jeff explains how he deduced Chang's wife left him.
jokes.punchline: The clues escalate perfectly: same shirt (plausible), esposa means liar (ominous), Post-it note speech bubble on a photo (devastating and specific).
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's genuinely exceptional jokes. The three-beat escalating list structure is textbook comedy writing: each clue is funnier than the last, and the final one — a Post-it note dialogue balloon on a photo saying 'Enjoy it while it lasts' — is specific, visual, sad, and hilarious simultaneously. It tells us everything about Chang's marriage, Chang's denial, and Chang's classroom. The 'esposa means liar' beat also pays off the Spanish-class framing. This is craft-forward writing at its best.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Sha-clackey!

jokes.text: We met at a salsa club. And, um, she loved the way I danced.
jokes.setup: Chang opens up about his marriage to Jeff.
jokes.punchline: The sincerity of Chang's vulnerability — revealing he was a dancer, that his wife fell for that version of him — is played completely straight and is quietly devastating and funny.
jokes.explanation: Good cringe/pathos moment. Chang's sincerity is funny because it's completely at odds with his classroom persona. The salsa club origin story humanizes him just enough to make his subsequent behavior more absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, so everyone's exempt from writing the essay?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: No, just you.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh.

jokes.text: You make no mistake about this, Winger. I pleasured that woman greatly. / Yeah. You look like you would have to.
jokes.setup: Chang insists on his masculine pride mid-emotional breakdown.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's response — 'You look like you would have to' — is a brilliantly ambiguous burn. It acknowledges Chang's desperation while also being kind of an insult dressed as a compliment.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional line. 'You look like you would have to' is working on multiple levels simultaneously: it could mean 'you look like someone who'd need to try hard to pleasure a woman' OR 'you look like someone who's desperate enough to make that claim right now.' Jeff's delivery of the line as a dry aside rather than an attack makes it even better. The 'I'm not surprised you said that' follow-up from Chang suggests HE doesn't fully know how to take it either. High originality in the ambiguity of the insult.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know what? I appreciate the offer, but I've got this handled.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Actually, you guys feeling guilty about something? Because now would be the perfect time to just do it for me.

jokes.text: Pickled bull testicle? / Are you offering or collecting?
jokes.setup: Chang offers Jeff something from a jar.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'Are you offering or collecting?' — the question implies Chang might be hoarding bull testicles as a hobby, which is funnier than whatever the real answer is.
jokes.explanation: Five-word punchline that's nearly perfect. 'Are you offering or collecting?' implies a whole disturbing hobby for Chang while also being a great deflection of the gross offer. Extremely economical and characterizes Jeff's ability to remain cool in absurd situations.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Maybe the rat is happy living with other rats now.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Yeah, Britta, be realistic.

jokes.text: Troy, sing. / The assignment is to train a rat to a song. / Yeah. Did you have to pick a duet?
jokes.setup: The biology assignment is to train a rat to respond to a song.
jokes.punchline: Abed points out that Troy chose a duet — meaning Troy will have to sing WITH the rat to train it, which creates maximum discomfort for someone who's afraid of rats.
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the Troy/rat subplot. The specific detail of a duet (implying Troy will be forced into close collaboration with the thing he fears) is a solid comedic choice. It also establishes Abed's matter-of-fact relationship with the absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You can't use those cards, Annie. Credit cards are a scam invented by the government to track your spending habits.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: And you can't use cash because cash is just paper, and paper comes from trees, and trees are monitored by the NSA.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: So the only logical solution is to barter exclusively in precious metals, which I happen to sell at competitive rates.

jokes.text: He did it. Good boy, Fievel. Commencing reward. / I have to open the cage. / Yeah, you don't have to warn me, I'm not afraid.
jokes.setup: The rat has completed its task; Abed announces he has to open the cage to reward it.
jokes.punchline: Troy immediately says 'you don't have to warn me, I'm not afraid' — which is EXACTLY the kind of thing someone who is afraid would say, especially unprompted.
jokes.explanation: Classic overcorrection joke. Troy's protestation is too specific and too immediate to be convincing. Works within the Troy characterization established earlier.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Oh, like, shut up.

jokes.text: Fievel. / Everybody shut up. / I'll kick all your asses, but you all have to come up here.
jokes.setup: The rat escapes. Troy panics.
jokes.punchline: Troy threatens to kick everyone's asses — but conditions it on them coming to him, because he's too scared to come down from wherever he's jumped up to avoid the rat.
jokes.explanation: Great physical comedy moment. The conditioned threat — 'I'll kick all your asses, but you all have to come up here' — perfectly expresses Troy's attempt to maintain tough-guy status while being paralyzed by rat fear. The structure (threat + undermining condition) is excellent. High character integration because this is 100% Troy.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You need a hook. Something that grabs people's attention right away. Like, 'Did you know that 90% of women prefer a man who can...' well, you know what I'm gonna say.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: No, I really don't.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Communicate. What did you think I was gonna say?

jokes.text: What about tonight? / Absolutely. / Oh, shoot. My Spanish study group has to get together every night now.
jokes.setup: Chang invites Jeff to hang out again tonight after agreeing to cancel the essay.
jokes.punchline: Jeff says 'absolutely' but immediately invents an excuse (the Spanish study group that Chang himself created with the essay) — revealing he's already trying to escape.
jokes.explanation: The irony is clean: Jeff uses Chang's own punishment as an excuse to avoid Chang. Good structural callback, though the execution is fairly light.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Eres muy feo.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Thanks, I appreciate that.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: That means you're ugly.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I know what it means, Chang. I'm just choosing to take it as a compliment.

jokes.text: Fantastic. That is fantastic. Everybody will be so happy. / Oh-oh-oh. I didn't say everybody. It's for my new friend Jeff.
jokes.setup: Chang cancels the essay for Jeff as a personal favor.
jokes.punchline: Chang clarifies the essay is cancelled only for Jeff — and by extension, Jeff is now on the hook to socialize with Chang to protect the rest of the group.
jokes.explanation: Good reversal. Jeff's celebration is immediately deflated and the trap is now set: he has to keep hanging out with Chang or the group gets punished. The 'Oh-oh-oh' is a nice verbal tic that makes Chang's sadistic pleasure clear.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Shakira, she's very formal Spanish. Tupac, he's street Spanish. Both dirty.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I'm not friends with them.

jokes.text: I suppose that will put you in an unenviable, uncomfortable position.
jokes.setup: Chang acknowledges Jeff is now trapped into befriending him.
jokes.punchline: Chang understands this dynamic completely and says so with almost clinical detachment — he KNOWS he's manipulating Jeff and doesn't care.
jokes.explanation: Good Chang characterization — his self-awareness about his own manipulation is funnier than pure obliviousness would be. Somewhat functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Remember that drink we had? The Blue Hawaiian?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, that was pretty good.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: BLUE HAWAIIAN! *chef's kiss* Those were the days, my friend.

jokes.text: Is there a rat in here? / I have no idea what you're talking about. / Abed. El Tigre.
jokes.setup: Chang notices something is off in the room.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's immediate denial is implausible; Abed gets a nickname 'El Tigre' presumably for his rat-wrangling abilities, which is delivered with complete seriousness.
jokes.explanation: 'El Tigre' as a nickname for Abed in a rat crisis is funny in its random specificity. The scene moves quickly but lands a couple of small beats.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You know what, Jeff? You're just a spray tan, a sweater vest, and a complete lack of self-awareness in a human suit.

jokes.text: Well, did you talk to Chang? Yeah, but it didn't do any good. My still head hurts from the yelling. My pupils are more sensitive to light because he yelled at me so much.
jokes.setup: Jeff claims he failed to get Chang to back off — covering for the actual deal he made.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's physical complaints are absurdly specific and escalate oddly — 'pupils more sensitive to light from yelling' is physiologically nonsensical in a funny way.
jokes.explanation: Jeff is fabricating fake symptoms to get sympathy while covering his deal with Chang. The escalating absurdity of the symptoms (head hurts → pupils more sensitive to light from yelling) is funny because it's medically nonsensical but delivered with conviction.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: The meek shall inherit the earth.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: But first, I'm going to kill you.

jokes.text: He probably found more rats and is very happy living with them. / Try to join the rest of us in reality, Britta.
jokes.setup: Britta tries to comfort Abed about the escaped rat.
jokes.punchline: Abed rejects her comforting fantasy and tells her to 'join the rest of us in reality' — a brutal ironic reversal since Abed is usually the one accused of not being in touch with reality.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character-based joke. Abed — the character who lives most in fictional and analytical worlds — telling Britta to 'join the rest of us in reality' is a perfect ironic reversal. It's funny on the surface but also characterologically rich: Abed is realistic about the rat's fate precisely because he doesn't emotionally project onto it, while Britta's sentimentality is the actual unrealistic response. 'The rest of us' also implies a larger community of realists that Abed is a member of, which is absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Your face is stupid!

jokes.text: Here comes Abed. He needs my help. I gotta get out of here.
jokes.setup: Troy sees Abed approaching after Fievel escaped.
jokes.punchline: Troy immediately tries to flee rather than face his fear or help Abed — directly contradicting his earlier bravado.
jokes.explanation: Decent callback to Troy's rat fear. His instinct to run rather than face Abed confirms the fear without belaboring it. Functional character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I've been divorced four times. I know what I'm talking about. When you break up with a group, you gotta do it clean. No Facebook messages, no group texts. You call each one individually.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: And whatever you do, don't let them keep the Foosball table. Trust me on this.

jokes.text: I believe that, uh, fusing brownies with the, uh, Internet is going to create the next Napster for brownies.
jokes.setup: Shirley is practicing her marketing presentation on brownies.
jokes.punchline: 'The next Napster for brownies' is an absurdly specific and nonsensical analogy — Napster disrupted music distribution, but brownies are physical goods, making this comparison hilariously meaningless.
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist business-speak joke. The specific choice of 'Napster' (music piracy platform) as a model for brownie distribution reveals how Shirley is cargo-culting tech startup language without understanding what it means. Very much of its era and still funny.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: La mujer tiene... muy grandes... 'software.'

jokes.text: Yawn! / Can't I just write it on cards? / No. Do you know anybody who reads from cards? No. No, you don't, and that's why.
jokes.setup: Pierce is coaching Shirley and dramatically expresses boredom.
jokes.punchline: Pierce — who will later literally give Shirley a card with a Nicholson quote to read — confidently declares that reading from cards is a presentation killer.
jokes.explanation: Gets a rewatch bonus because Pierce's confident anti-cards stance is immediately contradicted by his later advice to write the Nicholson quote on a card. His certainty is funny in both moments but funnier together.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Seven divorces? That's not the amazing part. The amazing part is that seven women agreed to marry him!

jokes.text: Also, you might consider a darker top. / Note taken. / Oh, and don't lock your knees. Never lock your knees. / You know what happens when you lock your knees? You die.
jokes.setup: Pierce gives presentation advice that escalates from fashion to physiology.
jokes.punchline: 'You know what happens when you lock your knees? You die.' Pierce delivers this with conviction — it's real advice (locking knees can cause fainting) but his escalation to death is absurdly dramatic.
jokes.explanation: 'You die' as the conclusion to a knees-locking warning is a great Pierce line — confident, slightly paranoid, and delivered as absolute fact. Good Pierce character voice.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I just need someone to lean on right now. My whole world is falling apart.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Of course, man. What do you need?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Can I... can I rest my head on your chest? I need to feel those pectoral muscles.

jokes.text: Second, when you wanna drive home a point, hand them a sandwich. / Try it. Hand them a sandwich. See? / Except that you're... You just dropped the sandwich as opposed to handing it to them.
jokes.setup: Pierce advises Shirley to hand the audience a sandwich to make a point.
jokes.punchline: Shirley drops the sandwich, undermining the technique before it can be demonstrated.
jokes.explanation: The 'hand them a sandwich' advice is already absurd as presentation coaching. The dropped sandwich adds physical comedy. Good but the transcript can't fully convey the visual timing.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You can't handle the truth! ...about our new moisturizing towelettes.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: These towelettes are moist. Devastatingly moist.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: And you people have the backbone of a chocolate éclair!

jokes.text: Try attention-grabbing words to wake up the audience, such as: Multiple orgasm. / Oh, no, no. I don't think that would fit into my message.
jokes.setup: Pierce advises Shirley to use 'attention-grabbing words.'
jokes.punchline: 'Multiple orgasm' as an example of an attention-grabber for a brownie presentation — Pierce says it completely straight.
jokes.explanation: Solid Pierce joke. His casual deployment of 'multiple orgasm' as standard presentation advice, with zero awareness of why Shirley objects, is good character comedy. Shirley's polite 'that wouldn't fit my message' is a great straight-woman response.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Now Annie, when you're up there presenting, you want to make sure you're making eye contact with the audience. Preferably the attractive members of the audience. And if anyone objects, just tell them you have a medical condition.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Also, wear something that shows off your... presentation skills, if you know what I mean.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Pierce, that's completely inappropriate!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Look, I'm just trying to help. But you can't tell anyone I said this, okay? Your mother would kill me.

jokes.text: These brownies are, uh... / Uh! / They, um... / Um! / These brownies are delicious. / They taste like... / Like. / That's not a filler word. Whatever, valley girl.
jokes.setup: Pierce has a method for eliminating Shirley's filler words: he shouts them back at her every time she says one.
jokes.punchline: The method works (she gets through 'delicious') but Pierce then shouts 'Like' at a legitimate use of the word 'like,' and defensively calls her a 'valley girl.'
jokes.explanation: Well-constructed running bit with a satisfying structural twist. The escalating embarrassment of each filler-word shout, followed by the successful 'delicious,' followed by the false positive on 'like' and Pierce's defensive 'valley girl' — the routine works because it has three phases: failure, success, overcorrection. 'Whatever, valley girl' is a great Pierce line because it reveals he was always a bit trigger-happy with the technique.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Troy, you've been acting really cool and dismissive lately. Did something happen?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I don't know what you're talking about.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: It's the chair, isn't it? You're sitting in a different chair in the study room and it's making you think you're cooler than us.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That's ridiculous.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: The corner chair, Troy. The corner chair gives you attitude. That's Sitcom Psychology 101.

jokes.text: The difference between usted and tú is a matter of formality.
jokes.setup: Chang teaches the class while Jeff has apparently gotten the essay cancelled for himself only.
jokes.punchline: The irony that Chang is now calmly teaching grammar while presumably torturing the rest of the class with assignments — the contrast with his earlier meltdown is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Setup for the subsequent jokes about how Chang uses the lesson. On its own, it's not a joke — it's a bridge.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: A true friend is someone who's always there for you, someone you can count on no matter what. Someone who will drop everything to help you out, cancel their plans, rearrange their entire life around your needs. That's what friendship is.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: And if they can't do that? Well, then they're not really your friend, are they?

jokes.text: You are old. / You are ugly. / No, you're not. Thanks, sir. / Shakira.
jokes.setup: Chang uses insults as example sentences in Spanish class.
jokes.punchline: He says 'You are ugly' to a student, then immediately adds 'No, you're not' — a correction that's somehow more insulting. Then 'Shakira' as a non-sequitur sign-off.
jokes.explanation: Good Chang classroom bit. Using 'you are ugly' as an example sentence is already Chang, but then correcting it with 'no, you're not' — which the student interprets as a compliment — is a nice miniature misdirection. 'Shakira' as a random exclamation is very Chang.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Look, I'm just saying, Abed's been acting weird all week. It's like he's lost his mind or something.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I mean, come on, the guy won't stop talking about how he's going to win a Grammy. A Grammy, Abed! You're not even a musician!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: And then he's like, 'Well, I could win a Tony.' A Tony? For what, exactly? Your documentary about blanket forts?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Next thing you know, he'll be telling us he's winning an Oscar. Then an Emmy. Then he'll be hosting The Price is Right.

jokes.text: You are dirty. / Dude. / Still formal but plural because while both are dirty, neither are my friends.
jokes.setup: Chang continues using insults as example sentences.
jokes.punchline: Chang explains the grammatical choice (formal plural) with a character note — 'neither are my friends' — which is both a grammar lesson and an admission about Chang's friendlessness.
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The grammar lesson structure allows Chang to reveal something genuinely sad about himself — 'neither are my friends' — while functioning as a correct explanation of usted vs. tú. The double function (grammar lesson + pathos/character revelation) is craft-forward writing. It also sets up the Jeff-Chang friendship subplot with new context.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Everyone, I'd like to introduce the real Green Day!

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Well, they're not really Green Day. But they play Green Day songs, and honestly, they're just as good.

jokes.text: Hope you guys are working hard on your essays. / Jeff already turned in his essay. / Great job. / As soon as you turn in your essays on Monday, there's gonna be a big-ass quiz, so study hard.
jokes.setup: Chang reminds the class about the essay — which Jeff had supposedly gotten cancelled.
jokes.punchline: The essay is apparently NOT cancelled for everyone else; now a quiz is added on top. Jeff's deception is revealed to the audience (and presumably the group will find out).
jokes.explanation: Good reveal structure. The audience sees Jeff's betrayal of the group take shape — the essay was only cancelled for him, and now there's a quiz on top. The 'Great job' to Jeff while announcing punishment to everyone else is a nice touch.

dialogue.speaker: Professor
dialogue.line: No note cards. You need to know this material cold.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: But I have everything organized here...

dialogue.speaker: Professor
dialogue.line: Cards. Now.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: No, please, I need—

dialogue.speaker: Professor
dialogue.line: This is a classroom, not a cue card factory.

jokes.text: Dude. Dude. Crazy night last night, man. That was crazy. When you go out with me, it gets crazy. That's the Winger guarantee.
jokes.setup: Chang approaches Jeff in the hallway acting like they're old buddies.
jokes.punchline: 'That's the Winger guarantee' — Chang has adopted Jeff's persona so completely that he's now using Jeff's catchphrase structure. The cringe of Chang trying to bro out with Jeff is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Good cringe comedy. Chang using Jeff's name as a branded guarantee shows how completely he's latched onto Jeff as his new best friend. The casualness of 'Winger guarantee' is both flattering to Jeff and deeply uncomfortable.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Brownies are just chocolate cake under pressure!

jokes.text: Bling. A-plus. Nice work, Winger. / I knew I could do it if I applied myself. / Cherry daiquiri. Cherry daiquiri.
jokes.setup: Chang grades Jeff's essay with an A-plus on the spot.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's smug response ('I knew I could do it if I applied myself') is immediately undercut by Chang's random non-sequitur 'Cherry daiquiri' — suggesting Chang is in his own world and the grade is not based on merit.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's self-congratulation is immediately revealed as hollow — the grade is friendship-based, not merit-based, which punctures his little moment. 'Cherry daiquiri' is a great non-sequitur Chang outro.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Here's Johnny!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I mean, here's the brownies!

jokes.text: Later. You devious clump of overpriced fabric and hair product. Speaking as one of the meek, soon as I inherit the Earth, you dead. You got a weird forehead. We're all very disappointed.
jokes.setup: The group discovers Jeff has been playing both sides — getting his essay cancelled while letting them suffer.
jokes.punchline: The group's insults pile on in escalating specificity: 'devious clump of overpriced fabric and hair product' (Britta), 'soon as I inherit the Earth, you dead' (Troy), 'you got a weird forehead' (unnamed), 'we're all very disappointed' (Annie).
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best sequences. Each character's insult is perfectly calibrated to their voice: Britta's is intellectual and cataloguing ('overpriced fabric and hair product'); Troy's is biblical and threatening ('the meek shall inherit... you dead'); the weird forehead one is petty and personal; Annie's 'we're all very disappointed' is the most devastating because it's the least dramatic. The escalation structure builds perfectly, with Annie's deflation as the final beat. High quotability on multiple lines. The sequence is funnier than any individual insult.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Thank you, Jeff. I'm canceling all group assignments.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Great!

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: However, I'm assigning you a new essay. The topic is: 'How I Manipulated My Teacher Into Doing What I Wanted.'

jokes.text: If anyone should be disappointed, it's me. What kind of a group threatens to kick someone out unless he helps them? / What kind of a person is asked to help other people and then helps himself?
jokes.setup: Jeff uses fake outrage to justify his behavior.
jokes.punchline: Britta nails him immediately with the parallel construction — 'What kind of a person is asked to help other people and then helps himself?' — turning Jeff's rhetorical device back on him.
jokes.explanation: Very well-constructed rhetorical reversal. Britta mirrors Jeff's question structure exactly, making it impossible for him to deny the parallel without also denying his own technique. The structure does the work here — matching grammatical forms creates the trap.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I've been thinking about what I've done, and I realize I need to make this right. The assignment I gave you all was impossible, and that was wrong of me.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: So effective immediately, I'm canceling it. Consider it done. Wiped from the record.

jokes.text: He's using fake outrage to justify leaving. / Fake outrage? Justify my...? / Yeah, that's it, I'm out of here.
jokes.setup: Abed analyzes Jeff's behavior in real time.
jokes.punchline: Abed accurately identifies Jeff's psychological manipulation technique; Jeff's sputtering response ('Fake outrage? Justify my...?') and then immediately storming out proves Abed right.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Abed joke and one of the episode's best moments. Abed live-commentating someone's psychological mechanism as they're deploying it — and being so accurate that the person's protest PROVES the point — is perfect meta comedy. The structure is airtight: naming fake outrage → Jeff sputters in (fake) outrage → Jeff leaves, confirming the prediction. Only Abed can deliver this joke. Very high character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Booyah!

jokes.text: Are you breaking up with the group? That's what you guys want. / I've been divorced seven times. Don't answer your phones and bury all your money in the backyard.
jokes.setup: Jeff threatens to leave the group.
jokes.punchline: Pierce — who has apparently been divorced seven times — immediately gives survivalist advice based on his divorces, treating Jeff's departure as equivalent to a marriage collapse.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Pierce joke. The reveal that Pierce has been divorced SEVEN times is itself funny, but his practical advice — 'don't answer your phones and bury all your money in the backyard' — treats the situation as a legal emergency with hard-won survival tactics. The specificity of 'seven times' and the matter-of-fact delivery make this a standout character joke. It's funny as a one-liner but also expands Pierce's backstory in a single sentence.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Your assignment is to write a self-aware title that describes exactly what you did.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: 'Self-Aware Title That Describes Exactly What I Did.'

jokes.text: Let's see, 'I took a computer class at tienda de manzana,' the Apple Store. Adorable. Keep going. / 'And the saleswoman had manzanas gigantes.' Ruined it.
jokes.setup: The group reviews Pierce's Spanish essay. The Apple Store ('tienda de manzana') is charming.
jokes.punchline: 'Manzanas gigantes' means 'giant apples' — but as a description of a saleswoman, it's clearly a crude sexual reference. 'Ruined it' is the perfect button.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly structured two-beat joke. 'Tienda de manzana' (Apple Store) is a genuinely adorable bit of intermediate Spanish and the 'adorable' response is earned. Then 'manzanas gigantes' takes the apple metaphor into sexual territory with plausible deniability (he might just be talking about apples!) and 'ruined it' is the definitive button. The word economy is excellent — the whole joke lives in two Spanish phrases and two English reactions.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'm sorry for calling you a 'sentient tax return.' That was below the belt, even for you.

jokes.text: Imagine being married to him? Seven times. Seven different women agreed to marry that guy. It's crazy.
jokes.setup: Pierce's essay has just revealed more about him.
jokes.punchline: The group processes Pierce's seven marriages — the sheer number and the impossibility of it happening seven times.
jokes.explanation: Callback to Pierce's seven divorces. Functional follow-through on the joke, but less impactful than the original because it just restates the absurdity without adding to it.

jokes.text: I'm so alone. I'm so lonely I wanna die.
jokes.setup: Chang approaches Jeff for companionship.
jokes.punchline: Chang skips subtlety entirely and states his emotional state with maximum directness: 'I'm so lonely I wanna die.'
jokes.explanation: Chang's total lack of filter is the joke. 'I'm so lonely I wanna die' is delivered as a conversational opener, which makes it darkly funny. The escalation from 'I'm so alone' to 'wanna die' in one breath is very Chang.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You know, Dean, I've been rewatching all the security footage from your office. There's a pattern.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: What? Abed, that's... why would you—

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You rearrange that desk chair at least seventeen times a day. Sometimes you just sit in it. For hours. Just... touching the armrests.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I—that's not—

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: And the filing cabinets? You run your hands along them when you think no one's looking. I'm looking, Dean. I'm always looking.

jokes.text: I just miss her so much. / Yeah. / I'm sorry. This is so stupid. No, no, no, it's fine, it's just... / Buddy, you know... I'm dumb. / I can see that you're hurting but I have to get to Accounting.
jokes.setup: Chang breaks down emotionally about his wife; Jeff tries to console him.
jokes.punchline: 'I can see that you're hurting but I have to get to Accounting' — Jeff abandons the emotional support mid-sentence to escape to class.
jokes.explanation: Good cringe deflation. 'I can see that you're hurting but I have to get to Accounting' is a perfect Jeff line — he acknowledges the emotional reality and immediately prioritizes his exit. The 'I'm dumb' self-flagellation from Chang before Jeff escapes is also good pathos/comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Why is the paint so runny? This isn't even real paint! It's like... it's like shooting someone with a bottle of Sunny Delight!

jokes.text: It's not like I'm hitting strip clubs with Professor Whitman. / You better not be. What?
jokes.setup: Jeff is explaining his absence to Chang.
jokes.punchline: Jeff mentions Professor Whitman's strip club habits as if it's common knowledge; Chang's surprised 'you better not be... what?' shows he didn't know about Whitman.
jokes.explanation: Quick joke that expands the world. The idea that Professor Whitman is known as a strip club regular is funny backstory for a faculty member. Chang's double-take ('you better not be. What?') is a good beat.

jokes.text: All I ask is for you to keep filling the void in my soul. / I'll have to think of something.
jokes.setup: Chang makes his emotional needs explicit.
jokes.punchline: 'All I ask is for you to keep filling the void in my soul' — stated as if it's a reasonable request. Jeff's 'I'll have to think of something' is a perfect non-commitment.
jokes.explanation: 'Fill the void in my soul' as a casually stated request is great Chang — it's both melodramatic and completely literal. Jeff's noncommittal response is the perfect deadpan counterpoint.

jokes.text: Let me rest gently on your pecs.
jokes.setup: Chang and Jeff's moment of emotional connection.
jokes.punchline: Chang's request to 'rest gently on your pecs' is physically intimate in a way that's completely unexpected and deeply uncomfortable — presumably he leans on Jeff's chest.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most memorable lines. 'Let me rest gently on your pecs' is exquisitely specific — not just 'lean on you' but 'rest gently' (the gentleness is somehow worse) on Jeff's 'pecs' specifically. It's simultaneously the most pathetic and most intimate thing Chang could ask. The word 'gently' does enormous comedic work. High economy, extremely high character integration, very quotable.

jokes.text: Best closer to a presentation, a Nicholson quote. You take a phrase from one of his films and you tailor it to your product. / You can't handle a moist towelette. Something like that, you know. But you can't use that one. That's mine.
jokes.setup: Pierce advises Shirley to use a Nicholson quote as a presentation closer.
jokes.punchline: 'You can't handle a moist towelette' — Pierce's adaptation of 'You can't handle the truth' — is both a genuinely good pun and immediately claimed as his own intellectual property.
jokes.explanation: Very good Pierce joke. 'You can't handle a moist towelette' works as a wordplay joke on its own, but Pierce immediately claiming copyright on it ('That's mine') is the funnier element — the idea that this is valuable IP worth protecting. Also sets up the callback when Shirley uses it in her presentation.

jokes.text: Just don't let anybody know I was involved.
jokes.setup: Pierce has just given Shirley extensive presentation coaching and advice.
jokes.punchline: Pierce asks not to be credited — but given how bad his advice has been (sandwich-handing, 'multiple orgasm,' reading from cards), this is funnier as a gift to Shirley.
jokes.explanation: Good Pierce character beat. The irony is that his advice is genuinely terrible, so being disassociated from it is actually the right call — but Pierce says it out of false modesty, not self-awareness.

jokes.text: Why do you care so much? / I don't. / Because Fievel's going to die. I'd rather die than listen.
jokes.setup: Troy is confronted about why he cares about the rat.
jokes.punchline: Troy denies caring — 'I don't' — but Abed's factual response ('Because Fievel's going to die') prompts Troy's 'I'd rather die than listen,' which is both a dramatic overreaction and an admission that he does care.
jokes.explanation: Good Troy character moment. His denial is immediately contradicted by his dramatic reaction, which is consistent with his earlier 'I choose not to be around rats because they're unpopular' reframing.

jokes.text: The exterminator is coming because of our rat. / I'd like to exterminate this conversation.
jokes.setup: Someone mentions an exterminator is coming for the rat.
jokes.punchline: 'I'd like to exterminate this conversation' — a dry wordplay pun using 'exterminate' in its secondary sense.
jokes.explanation: Functional pun. Gets a mild laugh from the wordplay but it's the kind of joke anyone could make — not character-specific.

jokes.text: What are you doing? / He's sitting in Jeff's chair so he's trying to act like Jeff. / Oh! Oh.
jokes.setup: Someone is sitting in Jeff's empty chair.
jokes.punchline: Abed immediately analyzes this as a behavioral attempt to embody Jeff — treating a seating choice as psychological mimicry, with the group's scandalized 'Oh! Oh.' as the reaction.
jokes.explanation: Good Abed meta-analysis joke. Only Abed would interpret sitting in someone's chair as behavioral mimicry and state it as fact. The group's scandalized reaction treats it as a devastating psychological insight.

jokes.text: I thought you might wanna help me. We are friends. / Abed, take it from a former prom king. Real friends help me with things, not vice versa.
jokes.setup: Abed asks Troy for help finding the rat because they're friends.
jokes.punchline: Troy's 'Real friends help me with things, not vice versa' — delivered from the authority of his former prom king status — is a perfect encapsulation of Troy's pre-character-development selfishness.
jokes.explanation: Very good Troy characterization. 'Take it from a former prom king' as a source of authority for a self-serving friendship definition is both funny and reveals Troy's arrested development. The 'not vice versa' is unnecessary but appropriately Troy-pompous.

jokes.text: Am I?
jokes.setup: Abed asks if Troy is really his friend; Troy gives his selfish definition of friendship.
jokes.punchline: After his speech, Abed's quiet 'Am I?' — a genuine question about whether they're friends — lands as an indictment. The pause before this line and after is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Two words that do an enormous amount of work. 'Am I?' reframes Troy's entire self-serving speech as evidence that Troy doesn't understand friendship. It's funny, it's quiet, and it cuts deep. The delivery would land as both a comedic punchline and a genuine emotional moment, which is the best kind of Community joke. Perfect economy — anything more would ruin it.

jokes.text: If he gets any nuttier, they're gonna put him on The View.
jokes.setup: Chang's erratic behavior continues.
jokes.punchline: Britta updates the running 'crazy = award/show' joke, upgrading from Grammy to The View.
jokes.explanation: Third iteration of the 'Chang's craziness = cultural recognition' joke. Funny as a callback but the joke is getting slightly tired by now. 'The View' is a funnier, more specific choice than 'Grammy' (since The View is associated with chaotic personalities). Diminishing returns.

jokes.text: They're not the real Green Day. Thought we should just rip that Band-Aid off quickly.
jokes.setup: The dean introduces Greene Daeye at the concert.
jokes.punchline: The dean preemptively deflates the disappointment by just stating the problem directly — 'They're not the real Green Day. Thought we should just rip that Band-Aid off quickly' — which is itself kind of a Band-Aid metaphor applied meta-textually.
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the Greene Daeye subplot. The dean's self-awareness about how disappointing this is — and his meta choice to just say it directly — is good characterization. 'Rip that Band-Aid off quickly' is a nice turn of phrase.

jokes.text: Hey. What's up? / Just got your text, man. Wanna hang out? / Because if you don't, I will fail you.
jokes.setup: Chang texts Jeff to hang out and Jeff shows up.
jokes.punchline: Chang adds 'because if you don't, I will fail you' — immediately revealing that the friendship is backed by coercion, undermining the casual 'hang out' framing.
jokes.explanation: Good Chang joke. The juxtaposition of 'wanna hang out?' (casual) with 'because if you don't, I will fail you' (threatening) in one breath captures Chang's character: he's genuinely lonely AND genuinely willing to abuse his power, simultaneously.

jokes.text: She said she didn't wanna talk to me. / I didn't tell her you wanted to talk.
jokes.setup: Chang says his wife doesn't want to talk to him; Jeff says he arranged for the band to dedicate a song to them.
jokes.punchline: Jeff reveals he didn't actually tell Chang's wife that Chang wanted to talk — he engineered a situation (the song dedication) that bypassed the communication block.
jokes.explanation: Good reveal of Jeff's scheme. The cleverness of using the band dedication as a neutral third-party communication channel is consistent with Jeff's manipulator-but-occasionally-good characterization.

jokes.text: 'The estimation of market value of brownies has...' / 'I, uh... Target group...' / Ms. Bennett, I'm afraid I have to ask you to put down the cards.
jokes.setup: Shirley begins her marketing presentation.
jokes.punchline: She's reading from cards (which Pierce warned against) and immediately gets shut down. The professor's formal 'I'm afraid I have to ask you to put down the cards' is delivered as if this is a grave matter.
jokes.explanation: Callback to Pierce's 'never read from cards' advice — ironically, he was right, even though he then gave her a card to read from. The professor's formal takeaway of the cards is a good sight gag (inferred).

jokes.text: Uh... l... Uh... [extended beat of Shirley paralyzed without her cards]
jokes.setup: Without her cards, Shirley freezes in front of the class.
jokes.punchline: The extended beat of Shirley unable to speak — just filler sounds — is the cringe comedy of watching someone fail catastrophically in public.
jokes.explanation: Classic cringe setup. The 30-second timestamp gap between [17:00] and the next line suggests an extended painful silence. The payoff (Shirley's speech) makes this worthwhile in context. Not funny on its own but crucial as cringe buildup.

jokes.text: They are wonderful. We all love brownies. They're delicious. / If you love brownies, you love life.
jokes.setup: After her frozen silence, Shirley abandons the script and speaks from the heart.
jokes.punchline: 'If you love brownies, you love life' — a sweeping philosophical statement that is both completely sincere from Shirley's perspective and totally out of proportion for a marketing presentation.
jokes.explanation: Great moment. 'If you love brownies, you love life' is funny because it's both overblown and completely authentic to Shirley — she's saying it with utter conviction. It's the inverse of the Napster analogy: instead of using jargon she doesn't understand, she's saying exactly what she means and it accidentally works. The simplicity after the technical language is the punchline.

jokes.text: Orgasmically delicious.
jokes.setup: Shirley has abandoned her script and is freestyling.
jokes.punchline: She uses Pierce's 'attention-grabbing word' advice — 'orgasmically' — but deploys it completely naturally, in a moment of genuine passion, which makes it both funnier and more successful than it would have been as a scripted line.
jokes.explanation: Excellent payoff to Pierce's coaching. The joke is that Pierce's terrible, inappropriate advice ('use the word orgasm!') actually works — but only when Shirley deploys it unconsciously and authentically. The word 'orgasmically' coming from Shirley in a school presentation is inherently funny, but the character logic (she's just describing her genuine feelings about brownies) makes it land harder than a straight shock gag. Very high economy — one word does enormous work.

jokes.text: Here's Brownie.
jokes.setup: Shirley has been talking about brownies passionately.
jokes.punchline: She produces an actual brownie and apparently names it 'Brownie' or offers it as a prop — the 'hand them a sandwich' Pierce advice repurposed into the brownie context.
jokes.explanation: Payoff to Pierce's sandwich-handing advice — Shirley has unconsciously integrated Pierce's coaching (give them a food item) in a way that fits her actual product. The fact that the audience apparently loves it validates Pierce's terrible advice by accident.

jokes.text: God, he's on my leg! He's on my leg!
jokes.setup: Fievel the rat has been loose and Troy has been desperately avoiding it.
jokes.punchline: The rat finally makes contact with Troy — and his shrieking reaction is the culmination of his elaborate rat-avoidance subplot.
jokes.explanation: Physical payoff for the rat subplot. The transcript can't capture the full physical comedy, but the dialogue ('He's on my leg! He's on my leg!') and the double-shriek are good. Gets impact credit for being the culmination of a well-established running gag.

jokes.text: He's getting a refill on his void.
jokes.setup: Someone asks what Chang is doing as he approaches the dance floor/group.
jokes.punchline: Abed repurposes Chang's earlier 'fill the void in my soul' request as a clinical observation — 'getting a refill on his void' — treating emotional need as a beverage service.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Abed lines. 'Getting a refill on his void' takes Chang's melodramatic language and reduces it to a customer-service metaphor — the kind of deadpan translation that is Abed's superpower. It's a callback that improves the original. Very high economy and quotability.

jokes.text: I got an A on my presentation and a lot of the credit goes to Pierce. And I had a great sandwich.
jokes.setup: Shirley reports her presentation success.
jokes.punchline: Giving Pierce credit (his advice was terrible) while specifically noting 'I had a great sandwich' — which the audience knows she dropped during the practice — suggests she finally executed the sandwich handoff successfully.
jokes.explanation: Good callback payoff. The 'great sandwich' is a small but satisfying resolution to the dropped-sandwich gag. Giving Pierce credit while specifically mentioning the sandwich is Shirley's sweet character voice.

jokes.text: I've been a horrible husband and I've been a horrible teacher. / And I'd like to thank my student, Jeff Winger, for showing me that and helping me fix my marriage. / No more 20-page essays due on Monday.
jokes.setup: Chang makes a public apology.
jokes.punchline: Chang thanks Jeff for 'showing me I'm a horrible person' — a sincere apology that is itself a backhanded compliment to Jeff — and then cancels the essays, suggesting the resolution was accidental on Jeff's part.
jokes.explanation: Functional resolution joke. The irony that Chang is thanking Jeff for showing him he's a bad person is mild but good. Mostly this is scene resolution rather than a standout comedic moment.

jokes.text: Although, Winger, you should write a one-page essay called: 'Taking Advantage of the Emotionally Vulnerable.' / Boo-yah.
jokes.setup: Chang resolves everything positively — then adds one final assignment.
jokes.punchline: Chang assigns Jeff a one-page essay with a title that precisely describes what Jeff did — 'Taking Advantage of the Emotionally Vulnerable' — mirroring the earlier 'Annie's Mistake' essay convention. 'Boo-yah' from Jeff acknowledges he deserved it.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best structural jokes. The callback to Chang's 'name the essay after what you did wrong' device is perfect — it was funny with Annie, it's even funnier here because (1) Jeff deserves it, (2) the title is devastatingly accurate, and (3) Jeff's 'Boo-yah' shows he accepts the judgment. This is the episode's best-structured callback: the callback deepens the original device rather than just repeating it. High structure score because the joke completes a narrative arc.

jokes.text: You did that for us? / Mm. Kind of.
jokes.setup: The group realizes Jeff's manipulation of Chang ultimately helped them.
jokes.punchline: 'Kind of.' — Jeff's honest-but-deflating admission that his help was accidental/incidental.
jokes.explanation: Good Jeff characterization in two words. 'Kind of' perfectly captures Jeff's self-serving accidental heroism.

jokes.text: I thought hanging out with you guys was the worst way to pass Spanish. / I was wrong. / Well, we're the best.
jokes.setup: Jeff makes a sincere admission about the group.
jokes.punchline: Britta's immediate 'Well, we're the best' — zero humility, complete self-assurance — is a good character-specific reaction to what should be a touching moment.
jokes.explanation: Functional resolution joke. Britta's immediate self-congratulation punctures the sentimentality in a way that's character-consistent.

jokes.text: Jeff, I'm sorry I called you a handsome hobo. / If you need help with that essay, you can rejoin the group.
jokes.setup: Britta apologizes to Jeff.
jokes.punchline: The apology acknowledges 'handsome hobo' as the insult it was — and immediately conditionalizes Jeff's return on him needing help with the essay Chang just assigned him.
jokes.explanation: Good callback that also reveals Britta's character: she won't just let Jeff back in; she uses his punishment as leverage. The 'handsome hobo' callback is satisfying.

jokes.text: What are you guys talking to me for? You go dance.
jokes.setup: The group has a moment of connection; Jeff sends them off.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's slightly dismissive 'you go dance' — refusing to get too sentimental — is good character voice. He's touched but won't show it.
jokes.explanation: Functional emotional deflection joke. Works to maintain Jeff's character voice in a sentimental moment.

jokes.text: I know your secret. I know about the chair.
jokes.setup: Abed approaches the person who was sitting in Jeff's chair.
jokes.punchline: Abed says 'I know your secret. I know about the chair.' — framing the chair-sitting as a dramatic conspiracy, adding an air of thriller-movie gravitas to what was a minor background gag.
jokes.explanation: Good Abed callback. He's treating the chair-sitting as a serious dramatic development, which is very Abed — narrative-framing mundane things as genre moments. 'I know your secret' is a great opener for what turns out to be about a chair.

jokes.text: Whoa. What model did you get? / It's the Tsunami 3000 Anniversary Edition. You? / The Devil's Drench XJ11. This is gonna be awesome.
jokes.setup: Troy and Annie encounter each other at what appears to be a water gun fight setup.
jokes.punchline: The elaborate model names for water guns — 'Tsunami 3000 Anniversary Edition' and 'Devil's Drench XJ11' — treat children's toys with serious enthusiast gravity.
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist detail. The specific model names ('Tsunami 3000 Anniversary Edition' especially) treat a water gun fight as a serious weapons procurement, which is funny. Classic Community tone — taking something trivial with complete earnestness.

jokes.text: Establish base camps. What part of the library do you want? / North east is closest to the drinking fountain, which is the...
jokes.setup: Troy and Annie are treating the water gun fight as a military campaign.
jokes.punchline: The tactical seriousness — 'establish base camps,' strategic analysis of the library geography — frames a fun activity as a war room operation.
jokes.explanation: Continuation of the water gun absurdism. 'Establish base camps' is a good military phrase applied to a college water fight. The drinking fountain strategic analysis suggests Troy is very into this.

jokes.text: Pierce, I hope that's the tiny gun that you throw at us to confuse us while you grab the giant gun taped to your back. / Seriously, this hardly seems like a fair fight.
jokes.setup: Pierce shows up to the water gun fight with what appears to be a tiny weapon.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's theory — that Pierce's tiny gun is a decoy for a 'giant gun taped to your back' — is both a reasonable Pierce theory and a classic misdirection setup. Britta's concern about fairness confirms the giant gun theory.
jokes.explanation: Good Pierce character joke. The idea that Pierce would bring a tiny decoy gun to a water fight to draw out the enemy before deploying a giant gun is 100% Pierce — competitive, paranoid, and way too into it. The theory being apparently correct (Britta's concern) makes it even better.

jokes.text: Oh, it's pepper water. Oh, it's pep... / Who puts pepper in water?
jokes.setup: Pierce fires his gun and Jeff/Britta get hit.
jokes.punchline: The gun contains pepper water — a creative escalation of the 'water gun' concept that's simultaneously more disgusting and less dangerous. 'Who puts pepper in water?' is a perfect deadpan callback to the absurdity.
jokes.explanation: Great episode-closing joke. 'Pepper water' as Pierce's secret weapon is exactly the right level of absurd — it's gross but not dangerous, creative but insane, and completely characterizes Pierce's approach to competition (he researched unusual ammo). 'Who puts pepper in water?' is a great button — it's the right amount of outrage.

tmdb_overview: Faced with an unreasonable amount of Spanish homework, Jeff's efforts to handle Señor Chang manage to help him, but not the rest of the class.
insight: Cringe-driven episode with 58 jokes in 24 minutes—escalation over punchlines.
